locator: Section 3; figure-caption and inline-mention instruction construction
finding: GPT-4 builds instructions from figure captions and, in 60K-IM, article sentences mentioning the figure. The instruction teacher does not inspect pixels.
implication: Teacher-side article knowledge can enter targets even when the student receives only a figure and question.
limit: A privileged teacher is not intrinsically defective; inspect each target for answerability. Local training-data directories are empty, so no local LLaVA-Med QA prevalence is claimed.

locator: Section 2; Table 2; Appendix H; arXiv:2406.19280v2
finding: GPT-4V sees both image and source text during reformatting. PubMedVision totals about 1.3M alignment/instruction entries. On the paper's shared LLaVA-8B setup, adding PubMedVision increases average medical VQA accuracy from 51.0 to 62.7.
implication: Image-aware denoising improves performance while leaving a testable question about information retained from captions.
limit: Do not describe this as a text-only teacher or imply that its quality controls are absent. Its limitations explicitly acknowledge synthetic hallucinations.

locator: II-B1, II-B4; V-E/Table IV; V-F; Appendix F
finding: Caption generation uses RoIs, metadata and medical knowledge; reasoning distillation supplies the known answer. RL changes the reported seven-task average from 61.8 to 61.5. Physician-rating exact agreement is 36%, within-one-point agreement 81%, and weighted kappa averages 0.64.
implication: Supports auditing visual premises independently of answer-conditioned rationales and headline averages.
limit: These are rating agreements, not disagreement about patient truth. Lingshu actively improves data quality and reports scaling benefits; it is not evidence that scaling cannot improve perception.

locator: Sections 2.2–2.3; multi-timepoint and volumetric evaluations
finding: Adds volumetric CT/MRI, whole-slide inputs, bounding-box localization and multi-timepoint CXR analysis. Volumetric prompts include report indications; up to 85 axial slices are processed.
implication: Supplying context and improving input coverage already form part of strong backbone development.
limit: Counters blanket claims that current systems only scale report text or cannot handle longitudinal evidence. Improved task scores alone still do not validate every generated claim.

paper: Comparative evaluation of generative AI models for CXR report generation in the ED
locator: Methods; Table 2; finding-level CT-referenced analysis
finding: In 478 selected ED patients with same-day CT, Lingshu had RADPEER 3b ratings in 616/1434 reads (43.0%) versus radiologists' 200/1434 (13.9%), while clarity was 88.0% versus 78.1%. AIRead had a 5.3% RADPEER 3b rate.
implication: Fluent reporting and diagnostic quality can diverge markedly.
limit: 1434 is 478 cases times three readers, not independent patients. This single-center, CT-selected cohort cannot identify training-objective causality or establish a general model ranking.

paper: Removing hallucinated references to non-existent priors
locator: Methods; MIMIC-CXR rewriting and CXR-ReDonE experiments
finding: Identifies prior-comparison targets in single-study report generation and retrains on reports with those references removed or rewritten.
implication: A direct medical precedent for supervision that requires unavailable evidence, plus an intervention on that supervision.
limit: This already establishes the missing-prior case. A new project must extend beyond rediscovering it, and preserve current findings while removing comparisons.

paper: DPO for suppressing hallucinated prior exams
locator: Section 5.2/Table 1; Section 5.3/Table 2
finding: A tested DPO setting reduces reports mentioning priors from 51.63% to 20.90%; clinical metrics show tradeoffs and SFT can perform better.
implication: Post-training can modify unsupported attribution, but suppression must be assessed alongside retained clinical accuracy.
limit: Prior-reference removal, DPO, and safety–utility tradeoffs are established prior art.

locator: Method/format and accuracy rewards; abstract and main evaluation
finding: GRPO with 600 training VQA examples reports average accuracy increasing from 55.11% to 78.22%. Reasoning references are not required; rewards evaluate final-answer correctness and output format.
implication: A useful positive result for RL efficiency, but a correct final answer does not independently validate the intermediate visual premises.
limit: These protocol-specific scores should not be compared numerically with other papers' averages. The reward design alone does not prove hallucinated reasoning.

locator: Methods; GRPO reward design and eight-modality evaluation
finding: Uses GRPO with answer/format rewards across eight imaging modalities and reports gains over its Qwen2-VL-2B base.
implication: Tests generalization over modalities and tasks, providing a stronger comparator than a single VQA dataset.
limit: Answer accuracy and interpretable-looking traces do not establish evidence sufficiency. Later versions change the base model; version-specific numbers must not be mixed.

locator: Reasoning synthesis, rejection sampling, and RL method
finding: Combines synthesized reasoning, rejection sampling and reinforcement learning for multimodal medical diagnosis and VQA.
implication: Adds a broad medical reasoning comparator to answer-only and distilled-CoT baselines.
limit: Accepting an answer-correct trajectory does not certify each observation. A causal audit is needed before attributing its gains to improved visual grounding.

locator: Training comparisons; text-only versus image-text RLVR
finding: Curated text-only RLVR gives larger gains on the tested public medical VQA benchmarks than the tested multimodal training recipe.
implication: Medical VQA improvement can come from reasoning or language adaptation without new medical images.
limit: Different training-data quality is a confound. This result does not mean the image is unused at inference or that medical vision training is generally unhelpful.

paper: Beyond Accuracy: Evaluating Visual Grounding in Multimodal Medical Reasoning
locator: Sections 3.2–3.5; Tables 1–4
finding: On 100 items each from four benchmarks, image-text RL changes accuracy from 56.5% to 58.8% while image sensitivity falls from 48.2% to 39.8%. The PathVQA negative VRS estimate has a confidence interval crossing zero.
implication: Direct evidence that answer scores and image-intervention metrics can diverge; a close evaluation predecessor.
limit: Random shuffling can preserve a correct label. Answer invariance plus visual wording is not sufficient to label an individual claim false. The small preprint study is suggestive, not a universal RL result.

paper: MIRAGE: The Illusion of Visual Understanding
locator: No-image versus explicit-guessing experiments; B-Clean
finding: Models produce visual descriptions without images, and some medical benchmark performance remains high. Explicit guessing instructions can change results substantially.
implication: An absent-image control is necessary, with prompts and failure handling specified.
limit: Does not distinguish benchmark contamination, question cues and legitimate medical knowledge by itself. Blank images, omitted images and corrupted images are different interventions.

locator: Figure 4; text-only analysis
finding: Text-only open-ended VQA-RAD/SLAKE accuracy spans about 11.5–33% in the tested models, while the new benchmark has much lower text-only performance. Four-choice text-only results on the new benchmark lie near 25%.
implication: Benchmark construction can reduce exploitable text cues.
limit: Open-ended 'chance' is not well defined. Low performance for a few text-only models does not prove complete freedom from all shortcuts or contamination.

paper: Act as You Think / Multi-Consistency Reward
locator: Section 3.4; perceptual and reasoning consistency rewards; Tables 6–8
finding: Med-Zero-17K and MCR explicitly address visual/reasoning/answer inconsistency. Training rewards include image-corruption behavior and reasoning–answer coherence.
implication: Grounding-aware RL is already established; compare against it directly.
limit: A text coherence judge or sensitivity to broad image corruption does not by itself verify a specific lesion premise. Consistency can coexist with a false premise.

paper: RadVLM with RL for reporting and grounding
locator: Matched thinking/non-thinking and RL experiments
finding: Task-specific RL improves report generation and visual grounding, while adding explicit thinking does not consistently help.
implication: Counters claims that all existing rewards only measure language or that longer reasoning is necessarily beneficial.
limit: Grounding and report metrics do not guarantee sufficiency of all diagnostic claims; compare with matched evidence access and training budgets.

paper: ChestX-Reasoner: step-by-step verification from daily reports
locator: Methods: RadRScore and RadRBench-CXR; mining reasoning chains
finding: Mines reasoning from reports and uses report-based process rewards. Its construction treats an unmentioned finding as normal/no disease under an explicit completeness assumption.
implication: A concrete instance where report omissions can become negative reasoning supervision, making an independent image audit valuable.
limit: An exposed assumption is not proof of an actual wrong label. The work includes clinical evaluation and useful gains; the next test is whether the omitted finding is present on the supplied image.

locator: UMRG/U-MRG-14K; reasoner and frozen segmentation expert
finding: Pairs implicit clinical queries and reasoning with pixel masks; RL trains a reasoner that prompts a frozen segmentation expert.
implication: Dense medical visual supervision and reasoning-grounding integration are feasible in bounded tasks.
limit: Segmentation success is not a complete certificate of diagnostic reasoning, but it contradicts an absolute claim that dense medical supervision cannot transfer.

locator: Sections 3.2–3.5; image-degradation token weights; Table 1
finding: Weights answer-aware teacher tokens by positive original-versus-low-resolution likelihood differences; reports 0.7058 average versus 0.6775 for OPD on the tested subsets.
implication: Counterfactual image-conditioned token weighting is already close prior art.
limit: Teacher dependence on broad image degradation is a model-specific proxy, not a ground-truth sufficiency label.

locator: Sections 3.1–3.5; Section 4.2 metric definitions
finding: Explicitly models evidence sufficiency, acquisition tools, verification, memory and confidence. Its unsupported-error metric requires an incorrect diagnosis and evidence not matching expert support.
implication: An evidence ledger, acquisition policy or sufficiency score alone is not a new contribution.
limit: Correct diagnoses with false visual premises require a separate audit, as do source-derived claims that are not supplied to the student.

paper: Spatial and factual RL for CXR reporting
locator: Equation 5; spatial/factual ablations and reward hacking analysis
finding: Uses regions and boxes with a spatial IoU gate before factual reward, and documents reward hacking.
implication: Joint spatial/factual process rewards are existing work; reference-report correctness remains a supervision assumption to audit.
limit: An anatomical box is not necessarily a lesion-specific causal explanation. An audit must test the claim's actual evidence requirement.

locator: Counterfactual view construction; answerability selector; 7358 triplets
finding: Uses original, lesion-removed and matched random-removal mammograms to train grounding and abstention behavior, with a separate answerability selector.
implication: Clinically targeted lesion removal plus an unrelated-region control is already very close prior art.
limit: Editing artifacts and the equivalence between removal and answer unavailability need validation. Extend to source provenance and missing clinical context rather than claiming lesion-removal novelty.

locator: Calibrated retrieval-size selection and preference tuning
finding: Controls factuality risk when selecting retrieved context and uses preferences to correct over-reliance on retrieval.
implication: Risk calibration and balancing context use already have medical multimodal precedents.
limit: Retrieved medical references are not the same as patient-specific evidence. Useful knowledge should remain available while unsupported patient facts are withheld.

locator: Dynamic audit construction; information omission/contradiction/delay; judge validation
finding: Uses 90 base instances expanded into 720 stress scenarios and audits diagnosis updates and evidence handling. Reported answer–reference judge validation has weighted kappa 0.32.
implication: Supports evaluating evidence arrival and revision, beyond final answers.
limit: 720 variants are not 720 independent patients; the reported judge validation does not establish expert validity for every dynamic-node label.

paper: Wound-image evaluation of HuluMed, MedGemma and chatbots
locator: Scoring framework and limitations, 20 cases
finding: Reports noncommittal outputs on a small wound-image set. The scoring rule automatically treats substantial hedging or structural ambiguity as incorrect.
implication: Illustrates an actionability concern and the need to inspect uncertainty policies.
limit: The rubric penalizes hedging by construction; this is not direct evidence of miscalibration, nor a controlled test of the proposed information-gap mechanism.

locator: PVI construction; defined predictor families and fitted null/input predictors
finding: PVI evaluates instance difficulty relative to a predictor family and data distribution; usable information can change under computation.
implication: Fit comparable input and null predictors on training data and validate on held-out cases before claiming a usable-information estimate.
limit: A frozen model's image-ablation gain is not Shannon MI, an expert sufficiency label, or an estimator of each entropy term.

locator: Main theorem; bounded monotone loss family
finding: Controls expected loss under the procedure's assumptions and calibration design.
implication: Define the clinical loss and nested output family before calibrating; a better score can improve efficiency.
limit: Expected population risk is not a per-patient promise, and standard CRC does not automatically control selective risk among non-abstained cases. A few hundred cases may be inadequate for rare-finding groups.

paper: Language Models with Conformal Factuality Guarantees
locator: Entailment sets and nested back-off construction
finding: Connects factuality to conformal prediction using less-specific outputs and calibration labels.
implication: A valid claim-filtering/back-off system requires appropriate labels and a precisely defined guarantee.
limit: A report omission is not a truth label; generic claim filtering is not automatically covered by the theorem, and hospital shift can break exchangeability.
